expect.name: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
expect.notes: The eastern base for this group of peaks, about 20 miles up the Duckabush River trail from Brinnon and roughly 1.1 miles and 1,700 ft above the Upper Duckabush camp, in a saddle a little over a mile from O'Neil Pass. Mount Steel and Mount Duckabush both stand directly above it, and Steel's less-travelled route from this side leaves the trail a few miles above the Duckabush camp and follows a small creek into an amphitheatre on the west side of the summit, where easy slopes lead to the top. Twenty miles with the Big Hump early on, a river ford in the upper valley that is genuinely hazardous outside high summer, and a trail that goes long stretches between clearings — recent accounts describe dozens of downed trees between the trailhead and the upper ford and heavy brush. Hart and LaCrosse Lakes a mile or two above make excellent extensions if you have the days. Season is mid-July through September.

expect.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
expect.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. days.note: From the Duckabush trailhead the trail is easy for the first ~2.4 mi, then climbs steeply and loosely over Big Hump before dropping back to the river. Camp at Ten Mile Camp (1,400 ft) beside the Duckabush River; there's a privy and multiple tent sites.

days.note: The trail continues along the river with overgrown, root-and-blowdown sections, then climbs in earnest toward the park's alpine zone. The final mile up to Marmot Lake / the O'Neil Pass junction is steep and exposed underfoot. Camp near O'Neil Pass (~4,950 ft) or at Marmot Lake, both of which put Mount Duckabush's south-side routes within striking distance.
days.title: Ten Mile Camp to O'Neil Pass / Marmot Lake high camp
days.objective: Continue up-valley to a high camp near O'Neil Pass or Marmot Lake, below Mount Duckabush

days.note: Drop packs at camp and head cross-country toward the peak's south side and South Ridge, mixing heather benches, talus, and short class 2-3 scrambling to the summit (6,254 ft). Route-finding is the crux more than technical difficulty; parties typically pick a line up broken rock and heather rather than a single defined trail.

expect.name: Belview and the Six Ridge camps — for Mount Olson only
expect.notes: This camp serves Mount Olson and nothing else in the zone. Olson is a scree, boulder and brush scramble at about 5,290 ft on the crest of Six Ridge, reached by a way trail that runs along the ridge top. Six Ridge itself is a primitive, unmaintained route linking the North Fork and South Fork Skokomish over roughly ten miles of crest, with blowdown, overgrown meadow, cairn-to-cairn navigation and more than fifty switchbacks on the eastern climb out of the river. It is a route-finding trip, not a trail walk, and it is the one objective here where getting lost is a realistic outcome. From Staircase you walk the valley trail to the Six Ridge junction, climb the switchbacks to the ridge and camp at Belview, then work west along the crest to the Olson way trail — a long two days in. From the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead you come in over Sundown Pass and approach from the west, which is the more commonly described way and puts McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake in reach as camps. NOTHING ABOUT THIS SHARES GROUND WITH THE SAWTOOTH OR FIRST DIVIDE PEAKS — do not plan it as an add-on to a Flapjack Lakes trip. Best late July through September once the meadows dry out; earlier the tread is buried and the route is next to impossible to follow, and in winter it should not be attempted.
expect.water: THE CRUX OF THIS RIDGE. Six Ridge is dry along the crest — there is essentially nothing reliable between the river and the tarns, and the ridge camps depend on small pools that shrink through the summer. Plan the day around the water, not the mileage, and carry a full load up the switchbacks.
expect.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not a quota area and effectively never full. Bear canisters are required. The ridge camps sit near or above the 3,500 ft fire line, so assume no fires. THE EASTERN SIX RIDGE TRAIL IS CURRENTLY CLOSED from the east edge of Belview Camp down to its junction with the North Fork Skokomish trail because of the 2025 fire, which for now leaves the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead as the only legal way in.
expect.capacity: A small old camp on the ridge, and further west the tarn camps at McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake; all tiny, none developed, and you will very likely have them to yourself

expect.name: Hester Lake and Myrtle Lake basins
expect.notes: This is the real base camp for Mount Price, and the only one. The Dingford Creek trail climbs steeply from the trailhead, passes the Myrtle Lake junction at a little over three miles, and reaches Hester Lake at around five and a half; beyond the junction the tread deteriorates noticeably and the crossings multiply. Price rises directly above Hester, and both the Hester Lake Route and the North Route stage out of this basin, so a party camping here is looking at their objective from the tent. Myrtle is the softer option if the day runs out early, but it puts you further from the peak. Snow lingers in these basins into June and the summit slopes hold it later, so July through early October is the window. With the road washout in place the whole trip is several miles longer each way, which pushes this from a fit party's long day firmly into an overnight.
expect.water: Both lakes are reliable all season, and Dingford Creek runs the length of the approach. Filter or treat.
expect.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead: fill it in, drop the stub in the box, carry your copy. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size is capped at twelve people. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the wilderness; both lakes sit just under that line so a fire is technically legal, but the ground is thin and the sites are heavily used, and stoves are the better answer. Seasonal fire bans override all of that and are common by August.
expect.capacity: A few established, flat tent spots at Hester Lake, enough for two or three parties before it feels crowded. Myrtle Lake, at about 3,780 ft and a couple of miles nearer the road, has a smaller number of rougher sites.

expect.name: Middle Fork Campground
expect.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. Book ahead, because this is the closest forest campground to Seattle and summer weekends fill months in advance. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.
expect.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
expect.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
expect.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.

expect.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
expect.notes: Worth reading before driving up with a plan to sleep in the back of the car, because the situation has changed and the change is not obvious on the ground. The lower valley is closed to dispersed camping, so the answer there is the campground or nothing. The Taylor River road is gated at the bridge at the end of the drivable road and its old roadbed is now the trail, so there is no driving in to a quieter spot. The upper road toward Dingford Creek is the one stretch still open to roadside camping, and it is currently cut by a washout at about road mile seventeen that closes vehicle access short of the Dingford Creek trailhead at 1,400 ft. That washout matters well beyond camping: with it in place the Mount Price approach and the Treen Peak path both gain several road miles on foot or bike each way, which turns two long days into overnight trips. Beyond the Dingford Creek trailhead the road has been gated to vehicles for years in any case. Road status in this valley changes year to year, so confirm the current state with the ranger district before committing; a party that discovers the washout at the barricade has lost the day.
expect.water: The river and its side creeks are within a few minutes of the road the entire length of the valley and run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used corridor.
expect.permit: This is the field that decides whether you can sleep here at all. A forest order closes dispersed camping along the road from the forest boundary up to the confluence of the Taylor and Middle Fork rivers, and along the Taylor River road out to the Snoqualmie Lake trailhead, including a quarter-mile strip on either side. That closure runs through the end of 2026 and covers essentially every pull-out parties used to use, including the ones nearest the Garfield approaches. Above the confluence, on the upper road toward Dingford Creek, roadside camping is not covered by the order. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or the interagency equivalent.
expect.capacity: Informal gravel pull-outs only, a vehicle or two apiece, nothing signed, levelled or established.

expect.name: Green Ridge Lake
expect.notes: The staging point for two of this zone's objectives and the one genuinely useful high camp on the north side of the valley. Treen Peak's Green Ridge approach starts here, and so does the East Peak ridge on the Garfield massif, which is the one part of that mountain with a walking line rather than a climb. Access is a faint unmaintained miners' and fishermen's path leaving the upper road at about 1,350 ft, roughly a mile below the Dingford Creek trailhead, climbing steeply northeast through timber; it is easy to lose in the first thousand feet and the brush is heavy when wet. Above the ridge crest at about 4,700 ft the ground opens into heather and scattered tarns and travel becomes pleasant. For most parties this is a contingency rather than the plan, since Treen goes in a long day when the road is open, but the road washout and the sheer gain from 1,350 ft make an overnight the sensible choice at present, and the ridge camp splits a brutal day into two reasonable ones. Season is July into October; the approach is snow-free early but the brush stays soaking until the summer settles.

expect.capacity: Small informal camp on the benches by the lake, room for a couple of tents. Nothing designated or maintained. Tarns on the ridge above take another tent or two.

overview.expect: Mount Hopper (6,120 ft) is a deep-interior Olympic summit in the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park, on the Skokomish–Duckabush divide near First Divide. Its line parent is Mount Steel (6,612 ft), about 1.96 miles west-northwest; Mount Duckabush, Mount LaCrosse, and White Mountain are also nearby. The peak is named for brothers Stanley and Roland Hopper, sons of a Singer Sewing Machine Company executive — Stanley took part in W. G. Steel's 1906 ascent of neighboring Mount Steel. The standard Class 2 line is straightforward climbing, but as of mid-2026 the historically standard Staircase/North Fork Skokomish approach is closed following the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire; the Duckabush River Trail toward Marmot Lake is the currently drivable alternative, at roughly double the approach distance.

expect.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park
expect.notes:
From Mowich Lake, follow the trail roughly 3 miles to Spray Park, then climb the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge. The ridge narrows above Observation Rock; continue along it until you find bivouac sites. High camp is normally somewhere between about 9,500 and 10,300 ft, at the point where Ptarmigan Ridge runs into the main cone below the Liberty Cap icefall. Higher camps are worth the extra carry because they let you look at the bergschrund and pick a line the evening before.

This is the shorter of the two approaches, and it is the one most parties would choose if the road cooperated. Since April 2025 the Mowich Lake road has had no public access, because the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge was closed permanently to cars, bikes and walkers; this start is unavailable until that changes. Even before that, the summer-only road usually opened after the route came into condition.

The approach to high camp is normally split over two days.
expect.season: May-Jul; the road to Mowich Lake is closed indefinitely, so this start cannot currently be reached by car
hazards: Bergschrund crossing off the Mowich Glacier, conditions-dependent
Loose rock descending from high camp onto the glacier
Icefall exposure below the Liberty Cap icefall near high camp
Verglassed rock and water ice on the upper mixed ground
Committing position with a descent by a different route — plan the carry-over
expect.baseFinding:
High camp is not the start of the climbing — and the mistake this route invites is treating the ridge you camped on as the ridge you climb.

From camp at around 10,000–10,300 ft you DESCEND, on loose rock or steep snow, onto the Mowich Glacier. If you are gaining height straight out of the tents along a rocky crest, you are still on the approach ridge.

The first real feature is the bergschrund, usually crossed by a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the centre. Above it the climbing is 40–45 degree snow for about 1,000 ft, and it ends in an obvious way: you run up under large rock cliffs. That is the signal to traverse left into an hourglass-shaped snow face rather than to keep going up.

The next decision point is a rock buttress at about 11,500 ft, where the route splits — left and around toward Liberty Cap between the buttress and the icefall, or right through mixed ground, a minor rock rib and the left margin of the Mowich Face to a second rock gully. Either way there is a short section of real rock or mixed climbing above 12,000 ft; if you have got that high on pure snow, you have probably drifted onto the Liberty Cap glacier ground.

Descent is normally the Emmons, not this route.

expect.name: White River, St Elmo Pass and Curtis Ridge
expect.notes:
Follow the Glacier Basin trail from White River Campground and leave it for St Elmo Pass (7,400 ft), about 4 miles in. Descend onto the Winthrop Glacier and traverse west toward Curtis Ridge, holding elevation. Cross Curtis Ridge, cross the Carbon Glacier, then climb moderate snow slopes onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point, where there are good bivouac sites.

This is the long way around the north side of the mountain and it shares its first half with the Liberty Ridge approach. It usually implies a car shuttle or, more often, a carry-over with descent by the Emmons–Winthrop back to White River — which conveniently is also the standard descent from the route itself.
expect.season: Available earlier in the season than the Mowich Lake road, at the cost of a much longer approach
hazards: Serac discharge from Willis Wall on the traverse between Curtis Ridge and the Carbon
Crevasse fields on the Winthrop and Carbon glaciers
Long committing traverse with no quick exit
Same bergschrund and upper mixed-ground hazards as the Mowich approach
expect.baseFinding:
Up to the Carbon Glacier this is the Liberty Ridge approach, and the same negative markers apply: leave the Glacier Basin trail rather than walking into Glacier Basin, lose height off St Elmo Pass rather than gaining it, and treat the ground under Willis Wall as a crossing rather than a place to stand.

Where it diverges: instead of turning up the Carbon toward the toe of Liberty Ridge, you continue west across the Carbon and climb snow onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point. If you find yourself gaining a defined rib immediately above the Carbon with Willis Wall right behind you, you have stopped at Liberty Ridge — Ptarmigan is further round to the west.

Once camped on Ptarmigan Ridge the start of the climbing is the same as from the Mowich side: down off the ridge onto the Mowich Glacier, then the bergschrund, then 40–45 degree snow to the base of the rock cliffs.

expect.name: Heart Lake Road kiosk pullout, trail 248 to 247
expect.notes:
From I-5 take SR 20 west toward Anacortes and Deception Pass, trend right onto Campbell Lake Road, then right at the Lake Erie Grocery onto Heart Lake Road.

About an eighth of a mile (roughly 0.2 miles) north of the grocery there is a gravel pullout on the east side of Heart Lake Road with an information kiosk. That is the Main Wall parking.

Take trail 248, which enters the woods on the RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE GATE. Follow it 5-10 minutes to a T junction with trail 247. Turn RIGHT — this is the junction that decides your day, because turning LEFT here takes you along mostly flat ground past a bench to Shady Hollow and the New Millennium Wall instead.

After the right turn, walk 2-5 minutes watching for a less-travelled UNMARKED trail on the LEFT. Take it uphill into the woods. It climbs short rock steps and then enters a clearing that gives a clear view of the Headwall and Snag Buttress routes. Keep going uphill and stay RIGHT at the final fork — the left branch leads to Ramp Wall. Fifteen to twenty minutes total.
expect.season: Year-round; Mount Erie is open all year and no seasonal raptor closure is currently in force
hazards: Unmarked junction — the left turn off trail 247 is easy to walk past
Short rock steps on the approach path
expect.baseFinding:
The trail meets the cliff at a prominent RIGHT-FACING CORNER, and that corner is the first pitch of Zig Zag. Where the path stops being a path is the route.

That corner is also the anchor point for the rest of Main Wall West — everything else here is found by walking along the base from it.

If you came out at a clearing looking across at a buttress rather than standing under a corner, you are still below the wall: carry on uphill and stay right at the fork.
